title: Demonstrate skills that relate to a safe and secure environment

lessons.title: Finding and reporting hazards
lessons.html:
Safety is everyone's job

A hazard is anything that can hurt people, animals or property. A risk is how likely it is that the hazard will cause harm. On a farm and at home there are many hazards. A safe person learns to see them and do something about them.

Common hazards

  • Machines: tractors, PTO shafts, augers and chainsaws.
  • Chemicals: pesticides, diesel, cleaning products and fertiliser.
  • Animals: bulls, cows with calves, snakes and bees.
  • Electricity: broken plugs, bare wires, wet cables.
  • Fire: veld fires, cooking fires, paraffin stoves and gas.
  • Falls: ladders, roofs, slippery floors and open trenches.
  • Water: dams, reservoirs and rivers where children can drown.
  • Heat and sun: heat stroke and sunburn when working outside.

What to do when you see a hazard

  1. Stop and think. Do not rush in.
  2. Warn people nearby.
  3. Make it safe if you can do it without danger, for example pick up a tool lying in a path, or put a sign by a wet floor.
  4. Report it to your supervisor or health and safety representative.

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 says employers must provide a safe workplace, and workers must work safely, follow safety rules and report unsafe conditions and injuries.

Safety signs

Colour and shapeMeaning
Red circle with a lineDo not do this (prohibited)
Yellow triangleWarning, danger
Blue circleYou must do this, for example wear ear protection
Green squareSafe place, first aid, emergency exit

lessons.title: Emergencies, fire and personal security
lessons.html:
In an emergency

Know these things before an emergency happens:

  • The emergency numbers. In South Africa, 10111 is the police and 112 can be dialled from a cellphone for emergencies. Know the farm's own numbers and the nearest clinic, ambulance and fire service.
  • Where the first aid box and fire extinguishers are.
  • Where the assembly point is.
  • Who the trained first aiders are.

When you call for help, say clearly: who you are, where you are, what happened, how many people are hurt, and stay on the line.

Fire safety

  • Never leave a cooking fire or candle burning alone.
  • Keep paraffin and petrol in proper closed containers, away from children and flames.
  • Do not burn rubbish on windy, dry days. Help keep firebreaks clear.
  • If clothes catch fire: stop, drop and roll.
  • If there is a fire, warn everyone, get out, and go to the assembly point. Only fight a small fire if you are trained and it is safe.

Basic first aid

If someone is hurt, make sure the area is safe for you first. Call for help. Do not move a person who may have a back or neck injury unless they are in danger. Press on a bleeding wound with a clean cloth. Wear gloves if you can, to protect yourself from blood. First aid must be learned through hands-on training by an accredited provider; this lesson does not make you a first aider.

Personal security

  • Lock doors, gates and store rooms. Do not leave keys lying around.
  • Report strangers, open gates, cut fences or missing animals to your supervisor.
  • Walk with others at night where possible and carry a torch.
  • Do not share your bank PIN or passwords. Be careful of SMS and WhatsApp messages that ask for money or personal details.
  • Keep children away from dams, machines and chemicals.

Key points

  • A hazard is anything that can cause harm.
  • Stop, warn, make safe if you can, and report hazards.
  • Know emergency numbers, first aid box, extinguishers and assembly point.
  • If your clothes catch fire: stop, drop and roll.
  • Lock up, report suspicious things and protect your personal information.
